food.text: Cereals were the most important staple of the Early Middle Ages. Barley, oats and rye were eaten by the poor, while wheat was generally more expensive. People of all classes ate grain as bread, porridge, gruel and pasta.

The Plan of Saint Gall, drawn between 820 and 830 AD, shows an entire Benedictine monastery. Its kitchens, brewery, stables and workshops sit beside the church and infirmary. The plan was never actually built.

Charlemagne's Capitulare de villis paid special attention to wine, especially how it should be made and stored. It was a text for managing the royal estates, with seventy chapters on lands, animals and administration.

Game, meat from hunting, was common only on the tables of the nobility. Pork, chicken and other poultry were the most common butcher's meats. Beef was less common because cattle required a greater investment in land.

The Capitulare de villis made an official called the iudex responsible for both the quantity and quality of the food produced on royal estates. It gave few instructions on how or where to grow crops, and simply stated quotas for some of them.

The Plan of Saint Gall was built up from five sewn parchments. The fourth parchment added an orchard and a garden at the top. The fifth was added at the bottom to make room for the livestock quarters.

The Capitulare de villis provided for selling fish and other goods that went unused because the king did not visit. The estates were expected to produce food for a court that might never arrive to eat it.

Slow and inefficient transport made the long-distance trade of many foods very expensive. Perishability made other foods impossible to transport at all. Much of what people ate therefore depended on what could be produced close to home.

Wheat, millet and rye were the most important crops of the Slavs in Poland. They also grew oat, barley, pea, broad bean, lentil, flax and hemp. Orchards held apple, pear, plum, peach and cherry trees.
food.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

food.text: The Capitulare de villis is much more specific about crops and animals than about everyday matters such as chickens. A comparison with the Brevium Exempla, which records actual audits, suggests it was largely aspirational and did not always correspond to reality.
Benedictine rules banned the meat of four-footed animals for everyone but the very weak and the sick. Monks got around this by declaring that offal and processed foods such as bacon were not meat.

Beginning in the 8th century, swine gradually became economically more important than cattle among the Slavs in Poland. They also kept sheep, goats, horses, dogs, cats, chickens, geese and ducks. Livestock keeping shifted as farming grew.
food.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

art.text: Under the Ottonian dynasty, art was mainly produced in large monasteries. Reichenau was the leading Western artistic centre in the second half of the 10th century. Its style used simplified, patterned shapes to create strongly expressive images, far from the classical aspirations of Carolingian art.
The wooden Gero Cross in Cologne Cathedral, made between 965 and 970, is both the oldest and the finest early medieval near life-size crucifix figure. It is a masterpiece of Ottonian sculpture.

Ottonian architecture, which survives mainly in churches, drew inspiration from Carolingian and Byzantine buildings. Emperor Otto I transported marble columns from Italy to use in his churches in Germany. Most large churches of the style were built with imperial patronage.

The Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire has a characteristic octagonal shape and is made of eight hinged golden plates. It was probably made in Western Germany for the imperial coronation of Otto I in 962, with later additions. It is now kept in Vienna.
art.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

art.text: Across early medieval Europe, metalwork was still the most prestigious form of art. One example is the jewelled Cross of Lothair, made about 1000 and probably produced in Cologne.

Ottonian churches were more than places of worship. They served as gathering halls for official ceremonies such as imperial coronations, and as burial places for members of the royal family. Their size and setting helped legitimize royal and Christian authority.
Art historians were reluctant to trust the records that dated the Gero Cross to 965-970. In 1976, dendrochronology, the dating of wood by its tree rings, confirmed the records were right.

The Church of Saint Pantaleon in Cologne stood on the site of a small 9th-century church. It was renovated by Archbishop Bruno, the younger brother of Otto the Great. Bruno was buried there in 965, and so was the wife of Otto II in 991.

The date of the Imperial Crown is disputed. It is most often dated to the second half of the tenth century, but John B. Freed argues its inscriptions are no earlier than the second half of the eleventh century. He links the Hezekiah plaque, which shows a king told he will be given fifteen more years of life, to Conrad III, who had become seriously ill with tertian malaria during the Second Crusade. Denise A. Kaiser argued instead that Otto II commissioned the crown and that the plaque refers to Otto I's recovery from a serious illness.
art.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

art.text: Ottonian architecture kept the Carolingian feature of apses at both ends of the church, and it drew on the Roman basilica. A few buildings, such as the apse of the abbey of the Holy Trinity at Essen, were influenced by the octagonal Palatine Chapel at Aachen.

Each of the two side plates of the Imperial Crown has three small holes. Chains with pendant jewels, called pendilia, probably hung from them. Byzantine imperial crowns had this feature, as shown in the mosaic portrait of Justinian I at San Vitale in Ravenna.
art.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: Slavic warriors in early medieval Poland were traditionally armed with spears, bows and wooden shields. Axes came into use later. Swords of the types popular throughout Europe in the 7th to 9th centuries were also used.
war.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

war.text: The Slavs settled the lands of Poland while invasions of Eastern and Central Europe by waves of people and armies from the east were destabilizing the region. The invaders included the Huns, the Avars and the Magyars.
war.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

war.text: Charlemagne became King of the Franks in 768 and began an extensive expansion of his realm. He eventually incorporated the territories of present-day France, Germany, northern Italy and the Low Countries, and linked the Frankish kingdom with Papal lands.

Around the year 940, the Gniezno gord was built in Greater Poland. It may have been placed there because the site was of great spiritual importance to the tribal community, so building and defending it would rally the local population around it.
war.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

war.text: By the late 8th century Byzantine military support in Italy had waned, and the Papacy looked to the Franks for protection. In 800 Pope Leo III owed a great debt to Charlemagne for securing his life and position.

In 951, King Otto I of Germany invaded the Kingdom of Italy and proclaimed himself king. He defeated the previous king and conquered Pavia in 961. He then went on to Rome, where he was crowned emperor in 962.

Archaeologists have found 7th- to 9th-century weapons and utensils in Pleszów and Mogiła, in the Kraków-Nowa Huta region. Other finds of the period, such as iron spurs and knives, come from Bonikowo and Bruszczewo in Kościan County.
war.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

literature.text: The surviving Old High German texts were written almost exclusively by clerics, mainly monks working in a small number of monastic scriptoria. They served almost entirely the purposes of the church, in a region that was still being fully Christianized.

The most famous work in Old High German is the Hildebrandslied, a short piece of Germanic alliterative heroic verse. Together with the Muspilli, it is the sole survivor of what must have been a vast oral tradition.

Scholars divide medieval German literature into two main periods. Old High German literature (750–1050) was the product of the monasteries and almost exclusively religious. Middle High German literature (1050–1350) came from the noble courts and focused on knightly exploits and courtly love.

Between the 6th and 9th centuries, Latin stayed in active use in Western Europe. Newly written vernaculars also rose and partly replaced earlier literary languages, and early Germanic literature, including Old High German, was among them.

Saints Cyril and Methodius worked in Great Moravia from 863. They introduced the original Slavic alphabet and translated Byzantine religious and political works. This became the foundation of Slavic literacy and literature, which soon profoundly influenced the Serbs.

In Old High German, the word literature has a broader scope than for later periods. It is not limited to imaginative works but covers everything written in the language, including prayers and theological works as well as verse narratives.

The earliest Old High German texts date from the second half of the 8th century. They were glosses and glossaries to help people learn to read Latin, and translations of Latin prayers, creeds and confessions for missionary or pastoral work among the lay population.
The Old High German period saw the first attempts to use the Latin alphabet for writing German. Otfrid of Weissenburg, writing c. 830, recognized that this was fraught with difficulty.
Translations and later adaptations of Latin Christian texts continued throughout the Old High German period. One example from the 9th century is Otfrid's gospel harmony.

Old High German texts were written down in isolated monasteries without prescriptive rules, so there is no standard Old High German. Each text shows a particular dialect or mixture of dialects, which are called Klosterdialekte, or monastery dialects.

Pre-Christian and non-clerical traditions survive in only a small number of Old High German works, such as the Hildebrandslied and the charms. Otherwise there is little surviving evidence of the oral culture that must have existed outside clerical circles.
Alongside the Hildebrandslied, the most famous works of the Old High German period include a heroic epic known as the Heliand. The period is reckoned to run until about the mid-11th century.

science.text: From the 8th century on, the Slavs in Poland worked their fields with oxen pulling wooden plows reinforced with iron. They cultivated fields as well as gardens within their settlements. This mix of animal power and iron fittings was the core farming technology of the region.
science.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

science.text: Early medieval Slavs in Poland burned forests to increase the land they could farm. The burning also served as fertilizer, because the ashes kept working in that role for several seasons. It was a practical way of turning woodland into productive fields.
science.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

science.text: The Slavs in Poland practiced crop rotation and a winter and spring crop system. After several seasons of use, they left a field idle so it could regain fertility. This shows an early understanding of how soil wears out and recovers.
science.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

science.text: The 10th-century Jewish traveler Ibrahim ibn Yaqub described the use of steam baths among the Slavs. Archeology has since confirmed that bath structures existed. His written account and the physical evidence agree.
science.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

science.text: Archeological research documents a steady growth in arable area over time, along with the resulting deforestation. Together with the written reports of Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, it is how we know the agricultural practices of the Slavs. Their farming visibly changed the landscape.
science.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

politics.text: The Treaty of Verdun in 843 split the Carolingian Empire and created the eastern Frankish kingdom. It grew into the Kingdom of Germany, which was made up of regions that became the stem duchies of Saxony, Franconia, Thuringia, Bavaria and Swabia.

After Charles the Fat died in 888, Carolingian rule in the Roman Empire ended. Regino of Prüm wrote that the parts of the realm "spewed forth kinglets", each electing one "from its own bowels". The last emperor of this period, Berengar I of Italy, died in 924.

In 773 Charlemagne crossed the Alps and invaded the Lombard kingdom, which covered all of Italy except the Duchy of Rome, Venice and the Byzantine south. By June 774 it had collapsed and the Franks were masters of northern Italy. Charlemagne then called himself king of the Lombards.

In 951, King Otto I of Germany, already married to Queen Adelaide of Italy, invaded Italy and proclaimed himself king. He conquered Pavia in 961 and went on to Rome, where he was crowned emperor in 962. The union of the Italian and German crowns with the imperial title proved stable.

The first Slavic state-like entity was the realm of King Samo, originally a Frankish trader. He became a Slavic leader by helping the Slavs defend themselves against Avar attackers, and his realm flourished from 623 to 658. It was probably a loose alliance of tribes and fell apart after his death.
politics.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

politics.text: Great Moravia was the most prominent Slavic state of its era and expanded greatly under Svatopluk I at the end of the 9th century. Yet it collapsed suddenly. In 906, weakened by an internal crisis and Magyar invasions, it ceased to exist entirely.
politics.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

politics.text: Slavic Carantania, centered on Krnski Grad (now Karnburg in Austria), was more of a real state than Samo's realm. It possibly developed from part of Samo's disintegrating kingdom. It lasted under a native dynasty throughout the 8th century and became Christianized.
politics.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages

politics.text: German kings had been elected since the 9th century, chosen by the leaders of the five most important tribes: the Salian Franks, Ripuarian Franks, Saxons, Bavarians and Swabians. Emperors often had their sons elected during their own lifetimes so the crown stayed in the family.

The imperial crown is probably from the late 10th century and may have been made in Western Germany for Otto I's coronation in 962. Historians disagree, however. John B. Freed argues it was made later for Conrad III, who had become seriously ill with tertian malaria during the Second Crusade and was hindered from carrying out his responsibilities from the end of August 1149 until April 1150. Denise A. Kaiser argued that Otto II commissioned it and that its plaque of the sick King Hezekiah refers to Otto I's recovery from a serious illness.
politics.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: In 920, King Henry of Germany liberated Utrecht from the Vikings, whose raids on the Low Countries had gone on for over a century. Around 879, the Viking leader Godfrid had arrived in Frisia at the head of a large force that terrorised the Low Countries and ravaged Ghent, Maastricht, Liège, Stavelot, Prüm, Cologne and Koblenz. Remains of Viking attacks dating from 880 to 890 have been found in Zutphen and Deventer.
politics.source_title: Netherlands in the Early Middle Ages

philosophy.text: Medieval philosophy as an independent project of inquiry began in two places: Baghdad in the middle of the 8th century, and the itinerant court of Charlemagne at Aachen in the last quarter of that century. In the Frankish lands, that meant France and Germany.
By imperial decree in 787, Charlemagne established schools in every abbey in his empire. These schools became centres of medieval learning, and the name Scholasticism is derived from them.
The first German philosophical controversy took place during the Carolingian Renaissance, in the year 848. Rabanus Maurus responded to Gottschalk of Orbais' doctrine of double predestination.

Rabanus Maurus, who lived from about 780 to 856, was a student of Charlemagne's preferred scholar Alcuin of York. He was known as "the first teacher of Germany" and served as deacon at the Benedictine Abbey of Fulda in Hesse.
Charlemagne's advisers Candidus, Peter of Pisa and Alcuin of York attracted the scholars of England and Ireland to his court. This produced the first significant renewal of learning in the West.

The Irish theologian and Neoplatonic philosopher Johannes Scotus Eriugena succeeded Alcuin of York as head of the Palace School. He translated and commented on the work of Pseudo-Dionysius, which was initially thought to be from the apostolic age.
A doctrinal dispute arose over whether God had predestined some people for salvation and others for damnation. Johannes Scotus Eriugena was called in to settle it.

Paschasius Radbertus raised the question of Christ's real presence in the Eucharist, asking how the host could be present in many places and times. He argued that Christ's real body is present at all places and times, veiled by the appearance of bread and wine, through God's incomprehensible power.

culture.text: The word Deutsche comes from the Old High German term diutisc, meaning 'ethnic' or 'relating to the people'. It was used for speakers of West-Germanic languages in Central Europe since at least the 8th century. After that time, a distinct German ethnic identity began to emerge among some of them.

On 25 December 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, the Frankish king, as Roman Emperor. This revived a title that had been dormant for more than three centuries since the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476.

In the 9th century, Charlemagne and his successors promoted an intellectual revival known as the Carolingian Renaissance. Some historians, such as Mortimer Chambers, argue it made possible later renaissances, even though the revival had already diminished by the early 10th century.
Christianity reached the area of modern Germany by 300 AD. By the time of Charlemagne, in the eighth and ninth centuries, the region had become fully Christianized.

The Treaty of Verdun in 843 split the Carolingian Empire and created an eastern Frankish kingdom. Its peoples included Franconians, Saxons, Frisians and Thuringi, who were referred to as Teutonici, or Germans, and sometimes as Franks. Ethnic identities shifted over the course of the ninth century.

In 962, Pope John XII crowned Otto of Saxony as emperor, reviving a title that had lapsed by 924. Known as Otto the Great, he was King of the Germans and became Charlemagne's successor, ruling lands first united as the Carolingian Empire.

Frisian settlers in the northern Netherlands and northwest Germany built a kingdom around the prosperous North Sea trading center of Dorestad. Because early Frisians and Anglo-Saxons came from largely identical tribal confederacies, Old Frisian is the language most closely related to Old English.
culture.source_title: Netherlands in the Early Middle Ages

culture.text: Louis the German was known at the time as Rex Germaniae, King of Germany, just as his brother was called King of Gaul. The titles distinguished parts of a theoretically single Frankish kingdom. It is not known whether they were meant to signify anything further.

Salian Franks who stayed in their homeland kept speaking Old Frankish, which by the 9th century had evolved into Old Dutch. Meanwhile, a Germanic language was spoken as a second tongue by public officials in western Austrasia and Neustria as late as the 850s. It vanished from those regions in the 10th century.
culture.source_title: Netherlands in the Early Middle Ages

culture.text: Regino of Prüm described the Carolingian realm's collapse after Charles the Fat's death in 888 in vivid terms. According to him, the parts of the realm 'spewed forth kinglets', and each part elected one 'from its own bowels'.

Independent of distant powers, the Slavic tribes in Poland lived a relatively undisturbed life. The cost was some backwardness in civilization. Until the 9th century the population was self-sufficient, and the few luxury items it used were imports.
culture.source_title: Poland in the Early Middle Ages
